table.title: [val] Code · CLI flags
table.md:
| Flag | Type | Default | Description |
|---|---|---|---|
| `--max-old-space-size` | number | `4096` | Sets the max memory size of V8's old memory section, in megabytes. |
| `--experimental-vm-modules` | boolean | `false` | Enables experimental ES module support in the `vm` module. |
| `-r`, `--require` | string | — | Preloads the specified module at startup. |
| `--inspect-brk=[host:]port` | string | `127.0.0.1:9229` | Activates inspector and breaks before user code starts. |

conditions.browser: Chromium (Playwright build), macOS system fonts, deviceScaleFactor 1

candidates.name: s1C
candidates.idea: Test whether S can retain its whole flags and two-line descriptions with slightly less horizontal travel.
candidates.label: gold

lineInfo.text: Sets the max memory size of V8's

whys: Flags and defaults stay whole, and descriptions read comfortably in two lines. The first viewport shows no description and cuts through the default column, so matching flags to explanations requires substantial horizontal scrolling.

Flags and defaults stay whole, descriptions read naturally in two lines, and the rows form a consistent rhythm. On the phone, the description is entirely beyond the initial view and the default is partially visible, so lookup requires substantial horizontal scrolling.
Flags and defaults stay whole, descriptions read naturally in two lines, and rows are consistent. The initial viewport hides the descriptions and cuts through the default column.

candidates.name: d2r1A
candidates.idea: Test a fitting layout that gives Type enough room to stay whole and shifts a little space toward Description. Flag identifiers and the address will still split, so the render must show whether the improved type and prose justify those breaks.
candidates.label: bad

whys: All headers fit on one line and the whole table is visible, but long flags, the address and experimental in the description are split. The narrow prose column also creates tall rows and substantial empty space.
All headers fit and the full grid is visible, but flag names, the address and experimental break across lines. The narrow description produces tall rows and makes comparisons laborious.
All headers fit, but long flags and the address fragment across lines, and experimental breaks inside the description. The tall rows contain substantial empty space.

candidates.name: d1r3A
candidates.idea: Test a scrolling layout that preserves complete flags and defaults while reducing description width and scroll distance; check whether the first description still fits in two lines.
candidates.label: gold

lineInfo.text: Sets the max memory size of V8's old

whys: Whole identifiers and defaults pair with readable two-line descriptions and even row heights. As in A, the initial viewport hides the descriptions and cuts through the default column; the extra ten pixels make little practical difference.

Whole identifiers, natural two-line descriptions and even row heights make the full table easy to scan. Like B, it requires substantial scrolling to reach the descriptions; the slightly wider text measure gives the first description a more comfortable break.
Whole flags and defaults, natural two-line descriptions and even rows make the full table easy to scan. The initial viewport hides the descriptions and cuts through the default column.

candidates.name: d3r3A
candidates.idea: Test a viewport-fitting compromise that gives Description enough room for its longest word and header. Flag names and the default address will still split, but prose should read more continuously.
candidates.label: bad

whys: The wider flag and description columns improve scanning within the viewport. However, the default column breaks its header, false and the address into fragments, while a long flag also breaks inside a word.

The description has a usable measure for the available width, but the Default header, false, the address and a flag name break awkwardly. Those splits undermine accurate lookup even though all columns are visible.
The description is more usable than in C, but the Default header, false and the address are fragmented, as are long flags. These breaks impair lookup.

Identifiers and defaults remain whole, and the narrower description column reduces horizontal travel. Its three-line descriptions produce taller, less even rows, while descriptions still start beyond the first viewport.

Identifiers remain whole and descriptions wrap naturally, though the narrower description creates taller, less uniform rows than B. The initial view still hides the description and cuts through the default column.
Flags and defaults remain whole, but several descriptions need three lines and create taller, uneven rows. The initial viewport still hides the descriptions.

candidates.name: contrast
candidates.idea: Equal columns give excess space to Type while forcing flag identifiers, the address, and description words to break; the result fits the viewport but impairs lookup and reading.
candidates.label: bad

whys: Equal narrow columns split the description header, flag identifiers, address and ordinary words. Very tall rows leave large empty areas under the short type and default values; the one-pixel overflow provides no useful benefit.

Flag names, the address and description words fragment across lines; the Description header also splits. Tall rows leave large empty areas, and the one-pixel overflow adds scrolling without useful relief.
Like C, this splits the description header, identifiers, address and prose into fragments. It also requires a small horizontal scroll despite its very narrow columns.

The default address stays whole and text avoids mid-word breaks, with only modest horizontal travel. Flags still wrap across several lines, descriptions are narrow, and almost none of the description column appears initially.

The address stays whole and flag names wrap at boundaries, while modest scrolling exposes the full table. Descriptions remain very narrow and tall, and almost none of that column is visible initially.
Headers and defaults stay whole, and the flags wrap at punctuation, but descriptions become narrow stacks of up to seven lines. The initial viewport shows almost none of the description column.
The table fits, but the narrow equal columns fragment flags, the address, the description header and prose. Long rows and large blank areas make scanning and comparison laborious.

The narrow columns split flag names, the address, words and the Description header. Very tall rows and isolated fragments make both lookup and continuous reading difficult, despite fitting the screen.
The description header, flag identifiers, address and prose break across awkward fragments. Very tall rows and narrow columns make scanning difficult.

d1.purpose: Provide a compact reference to CLI flags, their value types, defaults, and effects.
tasks: Find a flag by name or alias and read across its row.
Compare types and defaults between flags.
Read each description to understand when and how to use a flag.
relations: Each row connects a flag or its aliases to one type, one default, and one description.
The host and port placeholder belongs to the inspector flag; the address and port in its default form one value.
roles: The header labels four distinct fields; the flag column is the primary lookup key.
Type and default are short reference fields; description carries the explanatory prose.
The four body rows each describe one flag, with the short and long forms of require sharing a row.
keep_whole: Flag names and aliases where possible, including punctuation and the host-and-port placeholder.
The default address and port, type names, numbers, and inline code identifiers.
may_wrap: The require aliases can occupy separate lines while remaining in the same cell.
same_scale: All flag entries share one lookup role, and all descriptions share one explanatory role.
Type and default are both reference fields, but the longer default address needs more width than the type values.
d1.h_vs_v: A 360px viewport cannot preserve all unbreakable values and a useful description width at once. Fitting forces some identifiers or values to split and makes rows taller; scrolling can preserve them and reduce vertical fragmentation, at the cost of hiding right-hand fields initially.

d2.purpose: A reference for looking up command-line flags and understanding their types, defaults and effects.
tasks: Find a flag by name or alias.
Read the description to decide when to use a flag.
relations: Each row connects a flag with its type, default and description.
The short and long forms in the require row are aliases; the host and port are part of the inspect flag's syntax.
roles: Flag names identify the entries; Type and Default provide compact reference values; Description explains behavior.
The header row labels the four fields, and each remaining row is one flag entry.
keep_whole: Flag names and syntax where space permits.
Type names, default values and the address 127.0.0.1:9229.
Ordinary words and code references within descriptions.
may_wrap: The two require aliases between the aliases.
Long flag syntax only when the available width makes splitting unavoidable.
same_scale: The compact Type and Default columns should remain subordinate to the flag and description columns, while Default needs more room for the address.
All flag entries share one column scale, and all descriptions share another.
d2.h_vs_v: At phone width, fitting all four columns forces breaks inside identifiers or values and makes rows taller. Scrolling preserves reference values and gives descriptions more natural line lengths, at the cost of requiring horizontal movement to see the full row.

d3.purpose: A reference table for choosing and configuring command-line flags.
tasks: Find a flag by name or alias.
Check its value type and default.
Read what the flag does and compare related entries.
relations: Each row associates a flag with its type, default, and description.
The short and long forms of the require flag are aliases.
The host and port syntax belongs to the inspect flag; the address and port in its default form one value.
roles: Column headers identify the four attributes.
Flag names serve as lookup keys, although no row-header column is declared.
Type and Default are compact reference fields; Description explains behavior in prose.
keep_whole: Flag names and aliases, including their leading hyphens
The inspect flag's host and port syntax
Type names, numeric values, and the default address with its port
may_wrap: The two require aliases between the comma and the next alias
same_scale: Type and Default should remain compact but wide enough for their values.
Flag and Description need more space because they carry longer identifiers and prose.
d3.h_vs_v: A viewport-fitting table forces some identifiers or values to split and makes descriptions tall. Scrolling preserves lookup keys and defaults; additional width for prose reduces row height but increases horizontal travel.

analysis.strengths: Flags, types and defaults remain whole, making identifiers easy to scan and copy. Descriptions wrap at word boundaries.
analysis.faults: The description column needs up to three lines, making several rows tall. Initially the default column is cut off and descriptions are entirely off-screen.
analysis.spatial_logic: Gives each of the first three columns enough width for its longest one-line value, then limits the description to 200px to reduce scrolling.

analysis.strengths: Fits the viewport and keeps the Description header on one line. It gives flags and descriptions slightly more room than R.
analysis.faults: The Default header, false and the address split within words or values; long flags also fragment. Descriptions become narrow stacks, producing tall rows and slowing comparison.
analysis.spatial_logic: Protects the type column and divides the remaining width between flags and descriptions, leaving default too narrow for its contents.

analysis.strengths: Fits the viewport and keeps the short default false whole.
analysis.faults: Two headers split, as do flag identifiers, the address and description words. It is the tallest layout and its narrow text columns disrupt reading.
analysis.spatial_logic: Transfers a little width from flags and descriptions to default, but the gain is too small to preserve the longest default and creates new breaks elsewhere.

analysis.strengths: All identifiers and defaults remain whole, and descriptions fit in at most two lines. Even row heights and natural phrase breaks make the full table easy to scan.
analysis.faults: It requires the most horizontal scrolling. At first sight the default column is only partly visible and the descriptions are entirely off-screen.
analysis.spatial_logic: Retains one-line widths for the first three columns and spends additional width on descriptions to keep the rows compact.

analysis.strengths: Fits the viewport, keeps all headers on one line and preserves short defaults. Its wider default column makes the address less fragmented than in Q or R.
analysis.faults: Long flags split repeatedly, the address still breaks, and descriptions are very narrow. The resulting tall rows make lookup and comparison laborious.
analysis.spatial_logic: Allocates just enough width to keep headers intact, taking space from flags to give default more room.

analysis.strengths: The entire flag, type and default columns are initially visible. Defaults stay whole, descriptions read naturally in at most two lines, and rows have a consistent height.
analysis.faults: Several flag identifiers wrap, interrupting the primary lookup keys. Descriptions are initially off-screen and require horizontal scrolling.
analysis.spatial_logic: Uses the viewport width for the first three columns and puts a generous description column beyond it, accepting flag wraps to expose complete defaults.

rounds.insights: The fitted layouts expose all columns at once but cannot preserve all identifiers and the longest default at 360px. Their narrow descriptions also turn short entries into tall, fragmented blocks. The scrolling layouts preserve reading order better: S favors whole lookup keys, while U favors seeing all defaults immediately. A useful compromise can reduce scrolling from S while preserving complete flags; a separate fitted proposal must make an explicit trade-off among broken identifiers, defaults and prose.

analysis.strengths: Flags and defaults remain whole and are easy to scan.
analysis.faults: The first description takes three lines, making its row taller than the others. The initial viewport cuts through the Default column and shows no description.
analysis.spatial_logic: A wide flag column preserves identifiers, but the description is too narrow to give the first row the same rhythm as the rest.

analysis.strengths: All descriptions fit in two lines, defaults remain whole, and the first viewport shows the three lookup fields. Rows have a consistent height.
analysis.faults: Several flag identifiers wrap, interrupting their use as copyable or scannable units. Descriptions require scrolling.
analysis.spatial_logic: The flag column is compressed to make a compact scrolling table while keeping a useful first viewport.

analysis.strengths: The entire table is available without horizontal scrolling.
analysis.faults: Two headers and several words split; the address breaks across three lines. Long, uneven rows make comparisons difficult.
analysis.spatial_logic: Width is concentrated in the flag column at the expense of prose and defaults, producing a very tall table.

analysis.strengths: Flags and defaults remain whole, descriptions use at most two lines, and the rows have a regular rhythm.
analysis.faults: The first viewport cuts through Default and shows no descriptions. It requires more horizontal travel than s0B.
analysis.spatial_logic: The flag and description columns both receive enough width for comfortable reading, yielding the strongest full-table presentation.

analysis.strengths: The first viewport shows flags, types, and defaults; descriptions are readable in two lines and rows are uniform.
analysis.faults: Several flags wrap. The extra description width over s0B does not reduce row heights and increases horizontal travel.
analysis.spatial_logic: It favors prose width over flag continuity, without a clear overall benefit compared with s0B.

analysis.strengths: It fits the viewport and keeps all headers on one line. It is considerably shorter than s0C.
analysis.faults: Flags, the address, and a description word split awkwardly, making lookup and continuous reading difficult. Rows remain tall and uneven.
analysis.spatial_logic: More width goes to description than in s0C, improving the balance, but the available width remains insufficient for the table's code and prose.

rounds.insights: Scrolling preserves substantially more readable code and prose. S gives the cleanest whole-table reading, while s0B offers a useful first viewport and less horizontal travel at the cost of wrapped flags. Among the fitting layouts, T is more balanced than s0C, but both compromise identifiers and reading continuity. A further fitting allocation can test whether preserving the longest flag segment and the description header reduces damaging breaks.

analysis.strengths: Fits the viewport and gives flags enough room to wrap mostly at recognizable boundaries.
analysis.faults: The Default header, values and address break awkwardly; the narrow description also splits a word. Tall rows make scanning laborious.
analysis.spatial_logic: Space devoted to flags leaves the default column too narrow for even short values.

analysis.strengths: Compact scrolling width, readable descriptions and a viewport that shows the first three columns.
analysis.faults: The address breaks inside the value, and several flags wrap across lines.
analysis.spatial_logic: The first three columns nearly fill the viewport, but the default column falls short of the width its longest value needs.

analysis.strengths: Keeps flags and defaults whole, with readable two-line descriptions and even row heights.
analysis.faults: The initial viewport cuts through the Default header and address; the description requires scrolling.
analysis.spatial_logic: A wide flag column supports lookup by complete identifier, at the cost of pushing much of the default column off screen.

analysis.strengths: Keeps all identifiers and values whole, with comfortable descriptions and consistent rows.
analysis.faults: Like s1C, it cuts through the Default column at first sight and requires substantial horizontal scrolling.
analysis.spatial_logic: The extra description width adds scroll distance without improving the observed line count over s1C.

analysis.strengths: Shows flags, types and complete defaults together in the initial viewport; descriptions are readable after scrolling. No words break internally.
analysis.faults: Several flag identifiers wrap, so they are less immediately scannable than in s1C.
analysis.spatial_logic: The narrower flag column makes room for the complete default column within the viewport while preserving compact, regular rows.

analysis.strengths: Fits the viewport, keeps all headers on one line and gives short default values more room than s1A.
analysis.faults: Long flags and the address fragment severely, and the description breaks a word. The tall, sparse rows slow lookup.
analysis.spatial_logic: The relatively narrow flag and description columns distribute pressure across the table, but both carry content that needs more width.

rounds.insights: At phone width, the four columns cannot accommodate their longest unbreakable units together. Scrolling materially improves readability. s0B favors seeing flag, type and default together; s1C favors keeping complete flag identifiers on one line. Both have an even row rhythm, while the fitting options impose costly breaks and tall rows.

analysis.strengths: All content is visible in the full table, headers remain on one line, and descriptions read comfortably in two lines. The initial viewport shows all three identifying columns.
analysis.faults: Long flags wrap across lines, making exact command names slower to scan and copy. The description is entirely beyond the initial viewport.
analysis.spatial_logic: The compact flag column gives the first view a useful set of lookup fields, while the wider description column keeps the rows consistently shallow.

analysis.strengths: Like s2A, it shows the flag, type and default initially, with intact headers and two-line descriptions. The slightly wider description produces a natural first-row break.
analysis.faults: Long flags still wrap, and the extra width adds scrolling without reducing row heights or materially changing the reading experience.
analysis.spatial_logic: Its distribution closely matches s2A; the additional description width yields a small editorial benefit at the cost of a wider table.

analysis.strengths: Every flag stays on one line, making command names easy to find and read as complete identifiers. Descriptions remain readable and row heights match the other scrolling layouts.
analysis.faults: The first viewport cuts through the Default column, including the long address, and the table requires the most horizontal scrolling.
analysis.spatial_logic: Width is concentrated on the primary lookup key, trading a complete initial view of defaults for intact flag names.

analysis.strengths: All columns are available without horizontal scrolling, and the headers remain on one line.
analysis.faults: Several flags, the address and ordinary description words break inside their semantic units. Tall, uneven rows make both scanning and continuous reading difficult.
analysis.spatial_logic: The narrow viewport forces competing demands into four columns; the description and identifier columns become too narrow for their content.

rounds.insights: The scrolling layouts preserve readable descriptions and compact rows, but their main tradeoff is whether the initial view includes complete defaults or keeps flag identifiers intact. The fitting layout makes all columns immediately available but substantially damages reading through forced breaks. A fitting refinement should redistribute width toward flags and defaults while accepting a narrower description; its usefulness depends on the resulting rendered breaks.

bad.why: Several flag identifiers wrap across lines, making exact commands harder to scan and copy, while the description still requires horizontal scrolling.
Two long flag identifiers wrap despite the table requiring almost as much horizontal scrolling as s1C, which keeps them whole.
The narrow description column splits its header and ordinary words, producing very tall rows and difficult reading.
The default header and values split, including the boolean and address, making exact values difficult to read.
Two headers split, and flag identifiers and the address fragment across multiple lines.

contrast.why: Equal columns give excess space to Type while forcing flag identifiers, the address, and description words to break; the result fits the viewport but impairs lookup and reading.

synthesis.rationale: s1C keeps every flag and default value whole, with descriptions in two lines and consistent row heights. Its first viewport shows the flags and types but cuts through the Default column, so reading complete records requires scrolling. Layout T is the strongest fitting candidate because all headers remain whole and it has fewer measured within-word breaks than the other fitting layouts; nevertheless, it splits identifiers, an address, and description text. It is a constrained finalist for the fitting class rather than an equally readable alternative to s1C.

general: Protect exact identifiers and values from line breaks when readers need to recognize or copy them.
Allocate width according to content and reading task, and assess both the complete table and the initial viewport when scrolling is allowed.
Treat short, natural prose wraps differently from breaks inside words or code.
specific: A 225 px Flag column keeps all four flag entries on one line.
A 135 px Default column keeps the address whole; 76 px accommodates the Type values.
A 270 px Description column keeps all descriptions to two lines in the rendered candidates.

synthesis.tradeoffs: s1C requires substantial horizontal scrolling and initially cuts off part of Default; Layout P reduces total scroll distance but makes several rows taller. Layout T exposes all four columns at once, at the cost of fragmented code and prose and much greater height.
synthesis.uncertain: The best choice depends on how often readers need complete descriptions versus an all-column overview without scrolling. Layout T is the least compromised of the fitting candidates shown, but its broken identifiers and address may still fail acceptance for exact-reference use.

critique.good: All four fields are visible at once, and the row borders keep the associations clear.
critique.problems: Flag names, type values, the default address, and the Description header break unnaturally. The narrow prose produces very tall rows and makes scanning difficult.
critique.cause: The 110px flag, 66px type, and 80px default columns are too narrow for important values; the 103px description column also fragments prose.

critique.good: Types and defaults remain whole, descriptions read in manageable phrases, and the table is considerably more compact than A. The first viewport shows almost all three reference columns.
critique.problems: Several flag names wrap across lines, weakening the primary lookup column. The description is entirely beyond the initial viewport, so reading across requires scrolling.
critique.cause: The 155px flag column cannot keep the longest flag entries on one line. The 190px description column keeps the total width moderate but allows little prose per line.

critique.good: Complete flag names are easy to scan, reference values stay whole, and descriptions have comfortable line lengths. Consistent two-line body rows give the full table a calm rhythm.
critique.problems: The initial viewport cuts through the Default header and address, while the description is entirely off-screen. The wide table requires substantial horizontal travel to read across a row.
critique.cause: The 225px flag and 300px description columns preserve content well but make the table 737px wide.

critique.good: Keeps flag names, types and defaults whole; descriptions wrap naturally in at most three lines.
critique.problems: The first viewport cuts through the Default field and shows none of the descriptions. Several tall rows contain substantial empty space beside short reference values.
critique.cause: The 225px flag column pushes the 135px default column across the viewport edge; the 220px description column determines the taller rows.

critique.good: All four fields are visible without horizontal scrolling, and the type values remain whole.
critique.problems: Flag names, the address, the Description header and prose words split across lines. Very tall rows make scanning and following a record difficult.
critique.cause: The 127px flag, 75px default and 81px description columns are too narrow for their contents; the 360px total leaves insufficient space to preserve every field.

critique.good: The first viewport shows complete types and defaults alongside the flags. Descriptions wrap naturally, and the table requires less scrolling than the other scrolling designs.
critique.problems: Three flag identifiers wrap, including the inspector placeholder, making the primary lookup keys harder to scan. No description is initially visible, and the last row has considerable empty space below the flag.
critique.cause: The 155px flag column breaks longer identifiers; the first three columns together occupy 366px, placing the description just beyond the viewport.

critique.good: All flags and defaults stay whole, descriptions read naturally in two lines, and consistent row heights give the table a clear rhythm.
critique.problems: The first viewport cuts through the default address and hides the descriptions. The wide table requires substantial horizontal travel to connect a flag with its effect.
critique.cause: The 225px flag and 135px default columns extend beyond the viewport together, while the 300px description column increases the total width.

critique.good: Flag names and defaults stay whole, and descriptions wrap naturally. The lookup column is easy to scan.
critique.problems: The first description takes three lines, making its row taller than the others. The initial viewport cuts through the Default field and shows no description.
critique.cause: The 260px Description width creates the extra line; the 225px Flag width pushes much of Default beyond the viewport.

critique.good: Type and Default fit in the initial viewport, including the complete address. Description wrapping is natural.
critique.problems: Three flag names break across lines, including the inspector flag and its placeholder, weakening lookup. The first row is taller, and descriptions require scrolling.
critique.cause: The 150px Flag width is too narrow for the longer identifiers; the 250px Description width gives the first description three lines.

critique.good: All four fields are available without horizontal scrolling, and Type remains readable.
critique.problems: The Description header, prose, flag identifiers, and default address split unnaturally. Tall rows and narrow text fragments make both lookup and reading laborious.
critique.cause: The 116px Flag, 75px Default, and 92px Description widths cannot accommodate their content.

critique.good: Every flag and default stays whole, descriptions wrap naturally, and equal-height body rows give the table a calm, consistent rhythm.
critique.problems: The initial viewport cuts through Default and hides Description entirely. The full table requires substantial horizontal scrolling.
critique.cause: The 225px Flag and 135px Default columns extend beyond the viewport together; the 300px Description column adds further scroll distance.

critique.good: The initial viewport shows the flag, type, and almost all of Default. The shorter overall width reduces scrolling.
critique.problems: Long flags and the inspector placeholder break across lines; descriptions are more fragmented, and uneven row heights slow scanning.
critique.cause: The 155px Flag width splits identifiers, while the 190px Description width forces several descriptions to three lines.

critique.good: All flags, types, defaults and description words remain whole. The consistent two-line rows are easy to scan, and the descriptions read naturally.
critique.problems: The initial viewport cuts through the Default header and address, while the descriptions are entirely offscreen. The reader must scroll to complete each row.
critique.cause: The 225px flag and 76px type columns use most of the viewport; the 135px default column begins near its right edge.

critique.good: All four fields are present within the viewport, and the description has more room than in d1r2C.
critique.problems: Flag names and the address fragment across lines; two headers also break inside words. Tall rows and narrow prose make lookup and continuous reading difficult.
critique.cause: The 110px flag and 70px default columns cannot hold their longest values, and the 103px description column leaves too little room for prose.

critique.good: All reference values remain whole, and the wider description column gives the prose slightly more comfortable line breaks. The rows have a calm, consistent height.
critique.problems: The first viewport cuts through Default and its address, with no description visible. The additional table width does not reduce the row count or height compared with d1r3A.
critique.cause: The first three columns total 436px; the 300px description column adds 20px of scrolling beyond d1r3A without changing the two-line row pattern.

critique.good: The Default header stays on one line, and the inspector placeholder is less fragmented than in d1r3C.
critique.problems: Flags and the default address still split, while the description header and ordinary prose words break awkwardly. The long first row and uneven row heights make the table hard to scan.
critique.cause: The 116px flag and 75px default columns remain too narrow for their values; reducing the description to 92px severely fragments the prose.

critique.good: All headers and prose remain readable, and the type and default fields are largely visible on first sight. The table is narrower than the other scrolling designs.
critique.problems: Several flag names wrap, weakening the primary lookup column. The inspector default is cut by the initial viewport edge, and descriptions are entirely offscreen. Three-line descriptions make the rows relatively tall.
critique.cause: The 160px flag column wraps long names; the 220px description column produces several three-line cells. The first three columns together extend just beyond the viewport.

critique.good: The complete table is available without horizontal scrolling. The require aliases remain together, and type values are readable.
critique.problems: Description text forms very narrow, fragmented columns, with words broken across lines. Both Default and Description break in their headers, and the inspector address is split into three pieces. The resulting rows are exceptionally tall.
critique.cause: The 86px description and 70px default columns are too narrow for their contents; the 127px flag column also wraps long identifiers.

critique.good: Flag names and the inspector default remain whole in the full table. The narrower description column keeps total scroll width below d1r3A, while prose wraps at word boundaries.
critique.problems: Descriptions occupy up to three lines, leaving conspicuous empty space beneath the single-line reference fields. On first sight, the Default header and inspector address are cut off, and descriptions are hidden.
critique.cause: The 200px description column drives row height. The 225px flag column pushes much of Default beyond the viewport.

critique.good: Complete flag names and defaults are easy to scan in the full table. Descriptions wrap naturally into two lines, giving the rows a consistent, compact rhythm.
critique.problems: This is the widest design and requires substantial horizontal scrolling. The initial viewport cuts the Default header and inspector address and reveals none of the descriptions.
critique.cause: The 225px flag column preserves complete identifiers but pushes Default across the viewport edge; the 280px description column adds considerable width.

critique.good: The complete table fits the viewport, and the wider description column reduces height compared with d1r4B. Types remain readable.
critique.problems: Flag names and the inspector placeholder are fragmented, including breaks inside identifiers. The inspector address is split, both right-hand headers wrap awkwardly, and descriptions still contain broken words and narrow lines.
critique.cause: The 110px flag, 70px default, and 103px description columns cannot accommodate their contents or headers cleanly.

critique.good: All four fields are visible without horizontal scrolling, and the row borders preserve the flag-to-description relationships.
critique.problems: The description header, flag identifiers, type names, address, and ordinary words split awkwardly. Tall rows and narrow text fragments make scanning and comparison difficult.
critique.cause: All four columns are constrained: 110px for Flag, 65px for Type, 85px for Default, and 99px for Description are each below the width needed for important unbroken content.

critique.good: Flag names, types, defaults, and words remain whole. Descriptions wrap into manageable lines, and the rows retain a clear, consistent structure.
critique.problems: The initial viewport cuts through Default and shows none of Description. The long flag column leaves unused space in shorter entries, while reading an entire row requires horizontal movement.
critique.cause: The 225px Flag column preserves the longest syntax on one line, but with 76px for Type it pushes the 135px Default column across the viewport edge. The 200px Description column keeps total width moderate at the cost of several lines per description.

critique.good: Every cell fits on one line, making individual rows compact and preserving all identifiers and values.
critique.problems: Descriptions sit far outside the initial viewport, and the wide table requires substantial horizontal movement. The very long description lines spread related fields apart, while the initial view cuts through Default.
critique.cause: The 498px Description column accommodates the longest description without wrapping, expanding the table to 935px. The same 225px Flag and 76px Type columns place Default across the initial viewport edge.

critique.good: All four headers and fields are visible without scrolling, and the type values remain intact.
critique.problems: Flags, the address and ordinary description words break across lines. The tall rows and narrow text strips make both scanning and reading difficult.
critique.cause: The 100px flag, 78px default and 105px description columns are all too narrow for their content.

critique.good: The initial viewport shows complete type and default values alongside the flags. Descriptions have comfortable line lengths, and the table is relatively compact.
critique.problems: Long flags and inspect syntax wrap, making identifiers less immediate to scan. The descriptions start just beyond the initial viewport and require scrolling.
